transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Ariana Patel (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Jordan Reyes (Lyra Head of Data), Priya Menon (Lyra ML Eng), Samir Malik (Lyra CTO)

[00:00] Ariana Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh quick check-in today on the quality evals, we've got about 45 minutes. Marcus is with me from the SE team.
[00:17] Jordan Reyes: Yeah thanks Ariana, and thanks Marcus. We had a couple notes from last week, we ran the initial prompt set, saw some regressions on the disambiguation task.
[00:28] Marcus Chen: Right, so quick recap — we updated the scoring rubric to weight safety and factuality higher. I pushed prompt set v2 to the shared drive, link in the notes.
[00:40] Priya Menon: I pulled it down, noticed a couple prompts that seem to bias the model to over-specify, causing hallucinated entity mentions.
[00:52] Marcus Chen: Yeah that's consistent with what we saw. The model variant you're on for the POC has stronger generation but needs tighter guardrails. We can tighten the instruction templates and add a fallback classifier for hallucination detection.
[01:10] Samir Malik: Quick question — if we add the fallback classifier, does that affect latency a lot? Our product team is sensitive to 200 ms increases.
[01:24] Marcus Chen: It depends; the fallback can run asynchronously or as a light pre-check. In hosted flows there's a small overhead; with dedicated you can push that pre-check onto a separate worker node to keep p99 stable. We should benchmark.
[01:40] Jordan Reyes: Also we saw one case where the KV cache wording was transcribed as K-V cash in the logs, just FYI that the transcripts sometimes garble technical terms.
[01:50] Ariana Patel: Good callout, the eval scripts have a normalization step but we'll make sure technical tokens are mapped.
[02:05] Marcus Chen: On the regression runs — I propose two passes: 1) run with v2 prompt set and guardrails off to baseline; 2) run with guardrails on and fallback classifier enabled. We'll compare precision/recall and hallucination rate.
[02:25] Priya Menon: That sounds good. Also, for scoring - can we get a breakdown per intent? Right now aggregate score masks that disambiguation is the main offender.
[02:38] Marcus Chen: Absolutely, the spreadsheet has per-intent columns now. I added confidence bins and a qualitative tag column for 'hallucination', 'omission', 'irrelevant'.
[02:50] Jordan Reyes: We had a few prod failures last week — I'll extract the top two cases where the model invented dosages in medical context. Those are priority.
[03:03] Priya Menon: Yeah those two are scary. We'll share the logs and anonymize them.
[03:12] Samir Malik: From compliance perspective, we need to ensure SSO and audit logs capture these eval runs. Is that tracked?
[03:22] Ariana Patel: Yes, in the Private deployment the control plane logs eval runs; in Hosted we can enable extended audit logging for the project — we'll include the export. Marcus will grab the audit link.
[03:34] Marcus Chen: I'll attach the S3 export of logs to the drive and flag the eval runs.
[03:40] Jordan Reyes: Another question — we compared to OpenAI baseline for a handful of prompts and OpenAI had lower hallucination but higher cost. Have you folks seen similar tradeoffs?
[03:53] Marcus Chen: Yep. Tradeoff is typically cost/latency vs hallucination rate. We can push quantized variants on dedicated infra which narrows cost differences while maintaining quality.
[04:05] Priya Menon: For the guardrails, what's the easiest pattern? Is it instruction-only, or do you recommend a separate classifier + instruction combo?
[04:16] Marcus Chen: Best practice we've been using: instruction-level constraints + a lightweight classifier for edge-case rejection. Then a rewrite/fallback prompt that asks for structured output only. That reduces hallucination without too much latency impact.
[04:33] Jordan Reyes: Could you share examples of the rewrite fallback? The ones we saw before produced weird templated text.
[04:42] Ariana Patel: Sure, Marcus added examples in the doc under 'fallback_examples.md'.
[04:48] Marcus Chen: I'll paste two examples in the chat after the call — one for 'medical dosage' safe fail and one for 'unknown entity' template.
[04:58] Priya Menon: On metrics, can we get hallucination defined — is this model making up entities, or asserting false facts? We want both measured.
[05:11] Marcus Chen: Our scoring defines hallucination as any asserted fact that isn't present in the source context. We tag entity hallucination separately. The eval has both binary 'hallucinated? yes/no' and severity scales 1-5.
[05:28] Jordan Reyes: Ok that's helpful. In last run severity 4 cases were few but critical.
[05:35] Samir Malik: How long will the regression runs take? We have about 10k prompts in the suite.
[05:43] Marcus Chen: On hosted with current throttles it could take overnight; with dedicated reserved capacity we can run it in a couple hours. That's why scheduling a dedicated benchmark matters.
[05:55] Ariana Patel: For next steps we can turn the guardrails on selectively for the high-severity intents and run a focused 2k prompt pass this week.
[06:07] Priya Menon: That works for us. We'll prioritize the med/critical intents.
[06:14] Jordan Reyes: Another minor item — tokenization differences produced off-by-one in the scoring, causing slightly inflated token cost. Can you confirm the tokenizer variant?
[06:24] Marcus Chen: We're using the 'redwood-tokenizer-v2' which matches the model's tokenization. I'll add a mapping note to the sheet.
[06:33] Samir Malik: On security, we also need KMS integration for keys, can we get the RSA key rotation policy?
[06:42] Ariana Patel: Yes, for Private deployments we support customer-managed keys and rotation policies. I'll attach the security whitepaper.
[06:52] Marcus Chen: Back to guardrails — one practical tip: include negative examples in the prompt set so the model learns to refuse. Prompt engineering plus classifier is usually effective.
[07:05] Priya Menon: For the two prod failure cases, do you want us to redact patient identifiers before sharing?
[07:12] Jordan Reyes: Yes we'll anonymize. Priya will drop them in the secure drive folder.
[07:19] Ariana Patel: Perfect. We'll run regression with those cases included to see if the guardrails catch them.
[07:27] Marcus Chen: Also I'm going to run a metric called "regression delta" — percent change in hallucination rate per intent between baseline and guardrail runs.
[07:37] Samir Malik: If delta is small, we may need a different model variant or dedicated infra.
[07:44] Marcus Chen: Agreed. We'll produce a short executive table showing p95 latency, hallucination delta, and cost delta.
[07:54] Jordan Reyes: When can we expect the updated spreadsheet?
[07:58] Ariana Patel: I'll send v2 by Friday (2026-03-06). Marcus will follow up with regression artifacts by Monday (2026-03-09).
[08:08] Priya Menon: Great. For scheduling the dedicated latency benchmark — Samir, can you confirm availability week of 3/16?
[08:16] Samir Malik: Yes that's likely ok, I'll confirm by 3/10.
[08:22] Ariana Patel: Any other questions?
[08:25] Jordan Reyes: One last thing — licensing for Dedicated if we pivot. Can you send a rough monthly estimate?
[08:33] Ariana Patel: We'll send a ballpark in the follow-up; depends on GPU family and commit level. I'll include a couple options.
[08:41] Marcus Chen: I'll also include notes on quantization profiles we recommend per intent.
[08:47] Priya Menon: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[08:50] Ariana Patel: Thanks all, we'll recap next steps in the calendar invite.
[08:56] Meeting end.

Notes/links referenced: shared drive link (drive.redwood/example-evals), fallback_examples.md, security_whitepaper.pdf

Transcription notes: occasional mis-heard tokens (K-V cash -> KV cache), speaker boundaries sometimes off (Speaker labels merged), filler words and crosstalk present.
